KEY MESSAGE 1...Prolonged, heavy rainfall continues Wednesday 
leading to potential street and flash flooding, especially across 
western New England. 

We're approaching the period in which we expect the heaviest 
rainfall and thus the greatest flood threat in southern New England, 
generally Wednesday morning through Wednesday evening. In the mid 
levels, an anomalously strong low center is in the process of 
closing off over New York. Over the course of the next 12 to 36 
hours this neutral to negatively tilted trough will be slow to move 
east thanks to a blocking high over the north Atlantic, setting us 
up for a long duration rainfall event. It is a very moist and 
dynamic setup, a bit unusual for July in the northeast. Strong mid 
level divergence and upper diffluence will induce deep layer ascent. 
At the surface deepening low pressure moves up from the Mid Atlantic 
causing winds to back to the east and inducing a 30-40kt LLJ. This 
leads not only to convergence/rising air on the nose of the jet but 
also strong orographic/upslope flow into the high terrain of 
southern New England; principally the Berkshires but also the 
Worcester Hills. This will allow the axis of heavier rain over 
eastern NY to pivot over southern New England, while showers 
continue to exhibit training potential, especially over the 
Berkshires early. Given the very saturated atmosphere (PWATs over 
1.7") this is a setup conducive to big rainfall totals. As we've 
gotten into high-resolution guidance concern has increased for the 
potential of extreme amounts on the order of 5 to 7 inches where the 
heaviest bands set up. Unfortunately, exactly where they set up is 
nearly impossible to nail down short of a nowcast situation. 
However, the greatest threat continues to be western and central SNE 
where the Flood Watch is in effect. A more widespread 2 to 4 inches 
of rain is more likely for any given area. The most concerning 
period for western SNE will be this morning into the early afternoon 
when rainfall rates of 1 to 2 inches per hour are possible. 
Eventually that shifts into eastern MA in the later afternoon and 
evening/early overnight hours. So, the biggest concern for dangerous 
flash flooding (especially in urban and and poor drainage areas) 
will be for the Berkshire slopes/Hartford area during the morning 
commute. This then shifts toward the PVD-BOS corridor for the 
evening commute. Even given the extreme amounts, we continue to 
expect this to mainly be a flash flood/street flooding concern as 
opposed to river flooding, though we are keeping an eye on the 
rivers and streams. 

By Thursday the best moisture and dynamics have moved off but the 
vertically stacked low lingers leading to a damp, dreary day with 
lingering showers off and off throughout the day. As for 
temperatures, persistent easterly flow and thick cloudcover/rainfall 
will depress high temperatures into the low to mid 70s both 
Wednesday and Thursday. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...Cloudy weather into Friday with onshore flow 
and off- and-on light rain showers, to go along with cooler than
normal high temperatures.

The stubborn, slow-moving low pressure near southern CT with wound-
up, vertically-stacked upper-level closed low atop it begins to open 
up and fill as we move into Friday, eventually pulling offshore and 
away by Friday night. 

Unfortunately this means a continuation of cloudy, dreary weather 
with at least a modest onshore NE to N wind through the rest of the 
workweek. Guarded optimism that later in the day Friday could see 
some limited breaks in the cloudiness, but it's overall a cloudier-
than-not period. Off-and-on periods of showers can be expected as 
well too, but with the moist layer shown in model forecast RH cross 
sections being about 5000 ft or less in depth from the surface, 
these showers should prove light and could resemble more of a 
drizzle. Lows Thursday night are in the upper 50s to low 60s. Highs 
on Friday though are more challenging in that if we do get any late-
day breaks temps could reach into the low 80s. Better chance of that 
in western MA/CT, but otherwise have kept temps in the 70s, with 
even some upper 60s out over the Cape due to more clouds/onshore 
flow.

KEY MESSAGE 3...Generally dry weather with seasonably warm 
temps, but turning unsettled late in the weekend and especially 
into early next week.

Weak high pressure then begins to build in for the weekend, so we 
should see at least briefly drier weather return, though we could 
have to watch for lingering low clouds over the Cape and Islands. 
Confidence in this part of the forecast is lower-than-average 
though, as the issue is that most of the global ensembles show 
another elongated upper trough digging into the OH Valley with 
southwest flow aloft developing by Saturday. It's a pattern which 
could spell rain chances coming back into view in the SW flow aloft.
